doc.title: Tom Varner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 13, 2025

title: Ears, piano teacher Capitola Dickerson and slogging out horn technique
summary: Good ears but no natural technique; piano lessons with a jazz-loving teacher; hard work translating bebop language to the horn.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: You know our younger daughter played French horn for quite a few years. And I can recall listening to her, you know, when she was starting. And you described the French horn as “slippery.”
Yeah. It can be at first especially.
And we listened to her trying to find a pitch, to go up to a pitch and miss, and then finally get it. And my question to you is do you think you were blessed, born with good ears?

I did have good ears, but I did not have a naturally great technique. I was slipping and sliding like everybody else. I did take piano lessons, thank God, with a wonderful lady in Summit, New Jersey, Miss Capitola Dickerson. And she was a fantastic – she was a jazz lover and she was a fantastic just person and teacher, and she told me stories about going to see Billy Taylor on 52nd Street, and she told me about – she’d play me her Art Tatum 78s. And I was a terrible pianist, period. But I loved her, and she just instilled this love of music. And so that helped my ears for sure, the piano. And I had pretty good ears. I could pick out melodies and things on the piano and on the French horn. But the basic classical technique was still not easy. I had to really work at that. And then when you fast forward from age 14, 15 to 18 to translate the technique of the French horn on to being able to

play in that language of Miles Davis or a Clifford Brown or a Charlie Parker on a French horn, that was – required a lot of work. But it was just like kind of slogging work which after a while you kind of get it. You just have to like get through the difficulties of the articulation of how am I going to get this note to go from here to there the way it sounds like a tenor sax imitating Dexter Gordon or something. How the hell am I going to do that? Sometimes you just play, play, play – and you get it.
